title: Acts, again
tomorrow: Paul's 'charity is patient' wasn't written for a wedding. so who for?

segments.voice: Last week ended on John's word, abide: a branch that stays on the vine. Today the branches get up and walk out the door.

Every group project has someone everyone underestimates: the quiet one, the new one. Then they stand up to present, and the room goes still. In Acts, the room is the council in Jerusalem. Peter and John, two fishermen, are standing in front of it after a man who couldn't walk has gotten up at the Temple gate. The leaders look them over, and in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "understanding that they were illiterate and ignorant men, they wondered." They order them to stop speaking in the name of Jesus. And the two of them say they can't.
screen: `THE ONE EVERYONE UNDERESTIMATES.` → `TWO FISHERMEN BEFORE THE COUNCIL.` → `STOP. WE CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Their answer, in the same old translation: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." And the council notices one more thing, the reason behind the nerve: these two had been with Jesus. That's Acts in a sentence. It's the second half of Luke's story, and it opens with a promise: the Holy Spirit will come, and they'll be witnesses in Jerusalem, then farther, to the ends of the earth. Then it happens at Pentecost, and the sending begins. Look who gets sent. Not a team of experts. Fishermen. A man named Philip, picked to help hand out food, sent down a desert road to explain scripture to a stranger in a chariot. Ordinary people, moved along by the Spirit, often to places they didn't plan to go. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Latin Mass ends with the words ite, missa est, a dismissal, go. Some readers hear the very name Mass in that sending. Every Mass, in that reading, ends the way Acts begins. Out the door. Sent.
screen: `WE CANNOT BUT SPEAK.` · `THEY HAD BEEN WITH JESUS.` · `PHILIP, ON A DESERT ROAD.` · `ITE, MISSA EST.` · then, large: `SENT.`

segments.voice: Stand up and walk slowly, even across one room, for a minute. With each step, name a place you'll be today: a class, a job, a kitchen, a bus. Then sit for the rest, and ask to be useful in one of those places, or simply hope to be.
Acts. The Acts of the Apostles: ordinary people, sent by the Spirit, who could not stop speaking.
Your line: sent. Fishermen first, then a food server, then everybody after them. Catch you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: The council saw Peter and John as unlettered fishermen, yet they were sent. Acts is about ordinary people going where the Spirit sends them.

ite, missa est.meaning: Latin: go, it is the dismissal, said at the end of Mass
